17.title: The Twelve-Factor App
17.author: Adam Wiggins
17.why: Config, backing services and disposability are exactly the properties your Day 17 container needs; it predates LLM work and is still the clearest statement of why secrets live in the environment.

17.title: Multi-stage builds
17.author: Docker
17.why: The exact pattern in your Dockerfile — build deps in one stage, copy the artefact into a slim runtime — read it once so image size becomes a decision rather than an accident.

17.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025)
17.author: OWASP GenAI Security Project
17.why: This is the checklist a client's security team will actually hand you; knowing it before the meeting is the difference between leading the review and surviving it.

17.title: Configuring OpenID Connect in Amazon Web Services
17.author: GitHub Docs
17.why: The no-long-lived-keys CI pattern from Day 17's checklist, written out; it takes twenty minutes and it is the single clearest signal to a platform team that you have done this before.

18.title: Not what you've signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
18.author: Greshake, Abdelnabi, Mishra, Endres, Holz, Fritz (arXiv 2302.12173)
18.why: The paper that named the attack your RAG system is structurally exposed to; read §3 and §4 for the taxonomy, skip the rest on a first pass.

18.title: Everything tagged prompt-injection (161 posts, 2022–2026)
18.author: Simon Willison
18.why: Willison coined the term and has tracked every proposed defence since; skim the last two years to see which mitigations have actually held up and which were wishful. Look for the "lethal trifecta" framing — private data + untrusted content + exfiltration — it is the cleanest way to explain the risk to a client.

18.title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
18.author: Kwon, Li, Zhuang, Sheng, Zheng, Yu, Gonzalez, Zhang, Stoica (SOSP '23)
18.why: If you self-host, throughput is decided by KV-cache management — this is the paper behind vLLM and the reason your Day 18 break-even arithmetic needs a measured tokens/sec, not a vendor number.

18.title: Prompt caching
18.author: Anthropic
18.why: The single highest-leverage cost lever in the course — cache reads at 0.1× input price — and the mechanics dictate prompt ORDER: stable prefix first. That is a design constraint, not an optimisation.

19.title: Shape Up — Part 1, Shaping
19.author: Ryan Singer (Basecamp)
19.why: Read "Principles of Shaping" and "Set Boundaries" — appetite-before-estimate is precisely the move behind eval-first scoping, argued better than I argue it.

19.title: Product management at AWS: working backwards and the PR-FAQ
19.author: AWS Executive Insights
19.why: Re-read the press-release-first mechanism as a DISCOVERY tool — the PR is a forcing function for "what changes, for whom", which is discovery area six.

19.title: How to ask good questions
19.author: Julia Evans (Dec 2016)
19.why: Short and unusually concrete on the mechanics of getting a real answer rather than a polite one — which is the whole skill in a first discovery call.

20.title: Shape Up — Chapter 13, Show Progress
20.author: Ryan Singer (Basecamp)
20.why: Scopes and the hill chart — a language for "ugly and complete beats beautiful and partial" that a client can read off a wall.

20.title: Choose Boring Technology
20.author: Dan McKinley (Mar 2015)
20.why: The innovation-token argument, applied on a two-day capstone: you get one interesting choice, and it should be the thing you're demoing, not the database.

20.title: The Grug Brained Developer
20.author: Carson Gross
20.why: Funny, and quietly the best short piece on complexity discipline under deadline — read it the morning of a build day, not the week before.

21.title: Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure (SRE Book, ch. 15)
21.author: Google SRE
21.why: The blameless-writeup structure maps almost directly onto the case-study "hard parts" and "limitations" sections, which are the two that make it credible.

21.title: Writing for Engineers
21.author: Heinrich Hartmann (Apr 2022)
21.why: A working process for the kind of document you are writing today — audience first, structure second, prose last. The section on drafting from an outline is the part to actually apply.

21.title: How to Write Usefully
21.author: Paul Graham (Feb 2020)
21.why: "Important, novel, correct" as a test — apply it to your case study's hard-parts section and most of the padding falls out.

22.title: Principles of Instruction: Research-Based Strategies That All Teachers Should Know
22.author: Barak Rosenshine (American Educator, Spring 2012)
22.why: Ten principles, each with the evidence behind it — the closest thing to a checklist for the eight-beat lesson you're building, and it is free and short.

22.title: Cognitive load theory: research that teachers really need to understand
22.author: NSW Dept. of Education (CESE)
22.why: Why your live-coding pace loses people, stated as a mechanism — working memory holds about four chunks — rather than a platitude. This is what "too fast" actually means.

22.title: Teaching Tech Together — ch. 6 (A Lesson Design Process) and ch. 8 (Teaching as a Performance Art)
22.author: Greg Wilson
22.why: A whole free book on teaching programming, by the person who built Software Carpentry. Chapter 6 gives you learner personas and objectives; chapter 8 is live-coding technique. Those two chapters, not the whole book, this week.

22.title: The Carpentries Instructor Training curriculum
22.author: The Carpentries
22.why: An entire evidence-based instructor-training programme, open-licensed and readable. Skim it for the assessment mechanics — formative checks, minute cards, teaching demos — and steal the ones that fit your 60-minute lesson.

23.title: speaking.io — Tips for Public Speaking
23.author: Zach Holman
23.why: The most practical free guide to technical speaking there is — read "Prep for the Big Day" and "Deliver and Do Your Thing" the night before your one-take.

23.title: Teaching Tech Together — ch. 8, Teaching as a Performance Art
23.author: Greg Wilson
23.why: Live-coding technique specifically — pacing, typos, and why narrating your mistakes teaches more than a clean run.

23.title: Ideas for making better conference talks & conferences
23.author: Julia Evans (Jun 2016)
23.why: Her test — "say a new-to-your-audience thing in an understandable way" — is the one to hold your teach-back against. Also the argument for getting feedback from an actual target listener before you deliver.

24.title: Some blogging myths
24.author: Julia Evans (Jun 2023)
24.why: Kills the two beliefs most likely to stop you publishing — that it must be original and that it must be long — on the day you're deciding what to write.

24.title: My approach to running a link blog
24.author: Simon Willison (Dec 2024)
24.why: A working model of low-stakes, high-value technical writing from someone who has done it daily since 2003 — the realistic shape of a publishing habit you can keep past week two.

24.title: Learn In Public
24.author: swyx (Jun 2018)
24.why: The argument for making your learning exhaust visible, which is precisely what your 90-day plan is. "Create value for past-you" is also the best one-line description of what a trainer does.

24.title: Don't Call Yourself A Programmer, And Other Career Advice
24.author: Patrick McKenzie (Oct 2011)
24.why: Dated in its examples and still the sharpest thing written on framing your work in terms of what it did for the business — which is exactly the case-study and LinkedIn problem.
